source.title: The Few Govern the Many:Unveiling Few-Layer Dominance for Time Series Models
source.authors: Xin Qiu; Jun-Long Tong; Yi-Rong Sun; Yun-Pu Ma; Xiao-Yu Shen

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some table formatting is flattened or ambiguous, especially Table 4, so its individual numeric entries are not assigned where the layout does not support a reliable mapping.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly investigates whether increasing model size and training data improves time-series forecasting, and reports a scaling paradox: larger models often perform no better or worse. This challenges extending the claimed scaling behavior to time-series models, though it does not fit power-law curves.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own model-size and data-volume sweeps using forecasting MAE and MSE for time-series models. These results bear on the claim's extension to another modality, but the paper does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy or fit power laws. Values from Table 1 are identified as reproduced from other work and are excluded. Layer-representation and pruning results are excluded because they do not measure scaling behavior.
record.test_reason: The study trains two time-series model families (LLM4TS and TSFMs) at four scales from scratch or by fine-tuning. It reports held-out forecasting MAE/MSE, and MSE is the training objective. Across single-dataset, cross-dataset and out-of-domain settings, error mostly fails to fall, or rises, with model size. That is a direct result on whether scaling extends to the time-series modality (V5). It does not fit power laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also state that the paradox shows weak correlation with data volume, diversity and learning strategy, which leads them to attribute it to few-layer dominance rather than to data.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps time-series model scales and training-data volumes and evaluates forecasting MAE/MSE. It does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, fit power laws, or optimize parameter/token allocation at fixed compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scale outcome varies with learning strategy and evaluation setting: single-dataset versus cross-dataset learning, and in-domain versus out-of-domain evaluation. Increasing data volume improves errors but does not consistently reduce the gap between larger and smaller models.

fits_no_version.finding: Few-layer dominance: pruning most layers (keeping about 21–36%) and then fine-tuning matches or improves forecasting error. Inter-layer similarity is high in most layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In time-series transformers, most layers are redundant, and depth beyond a few layers does not reduce error.

record.problems: The study reports forecasting MAE/MSE rather than held-out pretraining loss and does not fit scaling curves or report exponents. Several scale results are presented graphically without exact values or uncertainty estimates. Table 4's flattened formatting makes some individual numerical assignments ambiguous.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's reproduced comparisons are cited from other work, not results generated by this study. Numerical entries from Table 4 were not separately cataloged where the flattened layout did not reliably associate values with models and metrics. Representation, pruning, classification, and efficiency results were omitted because they do not report the scaling behavior at issue.

untested.parts: Power-law form, exponents and fits are not assessed; only 3–4 sizes spanning about 1–2 orders of magnitude; compute axis not varied; no modalities other than time series. The data-volume sweep shows direction only.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.

missing.what: Numeric per-size averages for single-dataset and cross-dataset learning (both families); the mapping is confirmed by matching Table 6 'Original' columns.
Numeric OOD averages for the cross-dataset models by size.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 holds values reproduced from prior work and is correctly excluded. LLM4TS trainable parameter counts barely change between Tiny and Small, so the 'scale' there is mostly frozen backbone size. Results come from a single fixed seed with early stopping and no uncertainty estimates. Few size points, and no power-law fit.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy and power-law behavior in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted compute-optimal parameter/token trends.
No comparison of architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
The study tests scaling behavior in time-series forecasting, but does not fit or assess the shape of power-law curves, report exponents, or evaluate modalities other than time series.
No relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance is tested; forecasting errors are reported across model scales but are not predicted from pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared across parameter-counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Single-dataset time-series training (data-limited, 60K–15M observations), both families
relationships.reason: Error rises with model size (R1–R4), but data is likely the bottleneck; V5 presumes the other factors are not limiting. More data lowers error yet does not close the size gap (R5–R8).
relationships.display_finding: Error increased with model size, and additional data reduced error without closing the size gap, suggesting a data bottleneck.
